questions.q: A typical angiosperm anther is bilobed and dithecous. How many microsporangia (pollen sacs) does it have?
questions.explanation: Each lobe has two theca, so a typical anther is tetrasporangiate with four microsporangia.

questions.q: Which part of the carpel receives the pollen grains?
questions.explanation: The stigma is the landing platform for pollen grains.

questions.q: How many megaspores are formed from one megaspore mother cell by meiosis?
questions.explanation: Meiosis of the diploid megaspore mother cell gives four haploid megaspores, of which usually one is functional.

questions.q: Cleistogamous flowers:
options: Open widely and expose the anthers
Never open and are always self-pollinated, so seed-set is assured
questions.explanation: Cleistogamous flowers remain closed, so pollen falls on the stigma of the same flower and seeds are produced even without pollinators.

questions.q: A plant has 8 chromosomes in the gametes (n = 8). How many chromosomes will be present in a cell of its endosperm?
questions.explanation: Endosperm is triploid (3n) because it arises from two polar nuclei and one male gamete, so 3 x 8 = 24.

questions.q: A plant has 20 chromosomes in its megaspore mother cell. How many chromosomes are present in each nucleus of its mature embryo sac?
questions.explanation: All eight nuclei of the embryo sac are formed from a haploid functional megaspore by mitosis, so each has 10 chromosomes.

questions.q: Describe the structure of a typical anatropous ovule.
questions.answer: An ovule is attached to the placenta by a stalk called the funicle, and the junction is the hilum. It is covered by one or two protective integuments, leaving a small opening, the micropyle. The nucellus inside contains the embryo sac, and the basal region opposite the micropyle is the chalaza.
questions.explanation: The ovule becomes the seed after fertilisation.

questions.q: What is parthenocarpy? How can seedless fruits be produced in plants such as banana or grapes?
questions.answer: Parthenocarpy is the development of fruit without fertilisation. Banana is naturally parthenocarpic. Seedless fruits can also be induced by spraying the flowers with growth hormones such as auxins, which make the ovary develop into a fruit without seeds.
questions.explanation: Parthenocarpy is different from apomixis, which produces seeds.

questions.q: How many chromosomes are present in a normal human ovum?
questions.explanation: The ovum is haploid with 23 chromosomes, so fusion with a sperm restores the diploid number of 46.

questions.q: Which of the following is an accessory gland of the human male reproductive system?
questions.explanation: The seminal vesicles, prostate and bulbourethral glands are male accessory glands.

questions.q: The corpus luteum is formed from:
options: The remains of the ruptured Graafian follicle
questions.explanation: After ovulation the remaining follicular cells turn into the corpus luteum, which secretes progesterone.

questions.q: The process by which sperms acquire the capacity to fertilise an ovum after spending time in the female genital tract is called:
questions.explanation: Sperms undergo capacitation in the female tract before they can fertilise the ovum.

questions.q: Meiosis I of one primary spermatocyte results in the formation of:
questions.explanation: Meiosis I produces two haploid secondary spermatocytes, and meiosis II then produces four spermatids.

questions.q: If two ova are released in the same cycle and each is fertilised by a different sperm, the twins born are:
questions.explanation: Two different zygotes give fraternal twins, which are genetically different like ordinary siblings.

questions.q: Describe the phases of the human menstrual cycle.
questions.answer: The cycle has a menstrual phase with bleeding for 3-5 days, a follicular phase in which follicles grow and the endometrium regenerates, an ovulatory phase in which the ovum is released around day 14, and a luteal phase in which the corpus luteum secretes progesterone to prepare the endometrium.
questions.explanation: The average cycle length is about 28 days.

questions.q: Explain how the uterine lining is prepared for pregnancy after ovulation.
questions.answer: After ovulation the corpus luteum secretes large amounts of progesterone. This hormone maintains the endometrium, makes it thick and highly vascular, and stimulates its glands to secrete nutrients. These changes are essential for implantation and maintenance of pregnancy.
questions.explanation: If there is no fertilisation, the corpus luteum degenerates and menstruation follows.

questions.q: Reproductive health means:
options: A state of total physical, emotional, behavioural and social well-being in all aspects of reproduction
questions.explanation: According to the WHO, reproductive health is total well-being in all aspects related to reproduction.

questions.q: Intrauterine devices (IUDs) are inserted into the:
questions.explanation: IUDs are inserted by doctors or trained nurses into the uterus through the vagina.

questions.q: Which of the following infections can be transmitted by sharing of injection needles as well as by sexual contact?
questions.explanation: Hepatitis-B and HIV can spread through shared needles, blood transfusion and sexual contact.

questions.q: Family planning programmes were initiated in India in which year?
questions.explanation: India was among the first countries to start family planning programmes, in 1951.

questions.q: Diaphragms and cervical caps prevent pregnancy by:
options: Covering the cervix so that sperms cannot enter the uterus
questions.explanation: These rubber barriers are inserted into the female reproductive tract to cover the cervix and block sperm entry.

questions.q: In intra-uterine transfer (IUT), embryos with more than 8 blastomeres are transferred into the:
questions.explanation: Embryos with more than 8 blastomeres are placed in the uterus, as they have developed further.

questions.q: List three ways of creating awareness about reproductive health among adolescents.
questions.answer: Sex education in schools gives correct information about reproductive organs, adolescence and STIs. Audio-visual and print media, parents and teachers can provide accurate information. Awareness about contraception, safe sex and prenatal care also helps people make informed decisions.
questions.explanation: Awareness removes myths and misconceptions.

questions.q: Describe the steps of the in vitro fertilisation (test tube baby) technique.
questions.answer: Ova collected from the wife or a donor and sperms from the husband or donor are induced to form a zygote in the laboratory under simulated conditions. The zygote or early embryo with up to 8 blastomeres is transferred into the fallopian tube (ZIFT), and one with more than 8 blastomeres into the uterus (IUT), where development continues.
keyPoints: Embryo of up to 8 blastomeres into the fallopian tube
Embryo of more than 8 blastomeres into the uterus
questions.explanation: The first test tube baby was born in 1978.

questions.q: The trait that is expressed in the F1 hybrid when two contrasting traits are crossed is called:
questions.explanation: The trait that appears in the F1 is dominant, and the hidden trait is recessive.

questions.q: A normal human somatic cell has how many pairs of chromosomes?
questions.explanation: Humans have 23 pairs: 22 pairs of autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes.

questions.q: The phenotypic ratio in the F2 generation of a typical dihybrid cross is:
questions.explanation: Independent assortment of two gene pairs gives 9:3:3:1 in the F2.

questions.q: Haemophilia is:
questions.explanation: Haemophilia is a sex-linked recessive disease in which a protein of the blood clotting cascade is affected.

questions.q: Two phenotypically normal parents have a child with phenylketonuria, an autosomal recessive disorder. What is the probability that their next child will be affected?
questions.explanation: Both parents must be carriers (Aa), and Aa x Aa gives 1/4 aa.

questions.q: A child with blood group O is born to a father of group A and a mother of group B. What are the genotypes of the parents?
questions.explanation: The child's genotype is ii, so each parent must carry the i allele, making them IAi and IBi.

questions.q: What is a monohybrid cross? Give the genotypic ratio of the F2 generation in a cross between tall (TT) and dwarf (tt) pea plants.
questions.answer: A monohybrid cross involves one pair of contrasting characters. TT x tt gives Tt in F1, and selfing the F1 gives TT : Tt : tt in the ratio 1 : 2 : 1 in the F2, which is a phenotypic ratio of 3 tall : 1 dwarf.
keyPoints: Cross involving one pair of contrasting traits
questions.explanation: This ratio was the basis of Mendel's law of segregation.

questions.q: Distinguish between thalassaemia and sickle-cell anaemia.
questions.answer: Both are autosome-linked recessive blood disorders involving haemoglobin. In thalassaemia, a mutation or deletion reduces the rate of synthesis of one of the globin chains (a quantitative defect). In sickle-cell anaemia, a structural change in the beta globin chain produces an abnormal haemoglobin (a qualitative defect).
keyPoints: Thalassaemia: reduced synthesis of globin chains (quantitative)
questions.explanation: This is the key difference between the two haemoglobin disorders.

questions.q: Which type of RNA acts as the adapter molecule during translation?
questions.explanation: tRNA reads the codon through its anticodon and carries the corresponding amino acid.

questions.q: Griffith's transformation experiments were carried out on:
questions.explanation: Griffith used smooth (S) and rough (R) strains of Streptococcus pneumoniae and mice.

questions.q: Avery, MacLeod and McCarty showed that the transforming principle is:
questions.explanation: DNA-digesting enzymes stopped transformation, while protease and RNase did not, showing that DNA is the transforming principle.

questions.q: According to Chargaff's rule, in double-stranded DNA the ratio of purines to pyrimidines is:
questions.explanation: A pairs with T and G pairs with C, so the total purines equal the total pyrimidines.

questions.q: A prokaryotic 70S ribosome is made up of which subunits?
questions.explanation: The bacterial ribosome has a 50S large and a 30S small subunit (Svedberg units do not simply add).

questions.q: DNA fingerprinting is based on the polymorphism in:
options: Repetitive DNA sequences such as VNTRs
questions.explanation: Repetitive (satellite) DNA shows variation in the number of repeats between individuals, which gives a unique pattern.

questions.q: State the central dogma of molecular biology and mention the exception seen in retroviruses.
questions.answer: The central dogma says that genetic information flows from DNA to RNA (transcription) to protein (translation). In some retroviruses the flow is reversed, as RNA is converted into DNA by reverse transcription.
questions.explanation: The dogma was proposed by Francis Crick.

questions.q: Outline the steps of DNA fingerprinting and give one application.
questions.answer: DNA is isolated and cut with restriction enzymes, and the fragments are separated by gel electrophoresis. They are transferred to a membrane (blotting) and hybridised with a labelled VNTR probe, and the pattern is seen by autoradiography. It is used in forensic tests and for paternity disputes.
keyPoints: Isolation and restriction digestion of DNA
Hybridisation with VNTR probe and autoradiography
questions.explanation: The method was developed by Alec Jeffreys.

questions.q: Charles Darwin undertook the sea voyage on which ship?
questions.explanation: Darwin's observations during the voyage of H.M.S. Beagle shaped his theory.

questions.q: Alfred Wallace, who reached conclusions similar to Darwin's, worked in the:
questions.explanation: Wallace was a naturalist working in the Malay Archipelago.

questions.q: The Mesozoic era is popularly called the age of:
questions.explanation: Reptiles, including dinosaurs, dominated the Mesozoic era.

questions.q: Genetic drift refers to:
options: Random change in allele frequency by chance, especially in small populations
questions.explanation: Genetic drift is change in allele frequency due to chance events.

questions.q: Which pair of structures is homologous?
options: Wings of a butterfly and a bat
Eyes of an octopus and a mammal
Fins of a fish and wings of an insect
Thorns of Bougainvillea and tendrils of Cucurbita
questions.explanation: Thorns and tendrils have a similar origin (axillary buds) but different functions, so they are homologous.

questions.q: The eyes of an octopus and of mammals show similar structure although the animals are unrelated. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Structures with similar function but different origin are analogous and arise by convergent evolution.

questions.q: State the two key concepts of Darwin's theory of evolution.
questions.answer: Darwin proposed branching descent, meaning that species descended from common ancestors by modification, and natural selection. In natural selection, individuals with favourable variations survive and reproduce more in a given environment, so those traits become common.
questions.explanation: Darwin's theory rested on variation, struggle for existence and survival of the fittest.

questions.q: Explain adaptive radiation using Australian marsupials as an example.
questions.answer: Adaptive radiation is the evolution of different species from a common ancestor in a geographical area. Many Australian marsupials evolved from a single ancestral stock, spreading to different habitats and developing different features. Placental mammals show similar adaptations, so convergent evolution is seen between them.
keyPoints: Different species from a common ancestor
questions.explanation: Darwin's finches are another example.

questions.q: Which organism causes bacterial pneumonia?
questions.explanation: Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae infect the alveoli of the lungs.

questions.q: Amoebic dysentery (amoebiasis) is caused by:
questions.explanation: Entamoeba histolytica is a protozoan parasite of the human large intestine.

questions.q: Which of the following is a physiological barrier of innate immunity?
options: Mucus coating of the respiratory tract
questions.explanation: Gastric acid, saliva and tears are physiological barriers, while skin and mucus are physical barriers.

questions.q: A molecule of an antibody consists of:
options: One heavy and three light chains
Two heavy chains and two light chains
questions.explanation: An antibody is H2L2, made of two heavy and two light polypeptide chains.

questions.q: Morphine acts on the body by binding to specific opioid receptors present in the:
options: Central nervous system and gastrointestinal tract
questions.explanation: Opioids bind to opioid receptors in the CNS and gastrointestinal tract.

questions.q: A person with a deep, dirty wound is given an injection of anti-tetanus serum containing ready-made antibodies because:
options: Immediate protection is needed and the body cannot produce enough antibodies in time
The body can never make antibodies against tetanus
questions.explanation: Preformed antibodies give quick passive protection, as the body's own response would be too slow.

questions.q: Differentiate between active and passive immunity.
questions.answer: In active immunity, the body produces its own antibodies after exposure to antigens, either from infection or vaccination; it is slow and has a memory. In passive immunity, ready-made antibodies are given from outside, for example through colostrum, so protection is quick but short-lived and without memory.
keyPoints: Active: own antibodies, slow, has memory
Passive: ready-made antibodies, quick, no memory
questions.explanation: Vaccination gives active immunity.

questions.q: Describe briefly the life cycle of Plasmodium in the human body.
questions.answer: Sporozoites enter the human body through the mosquito bite and go to the liver cells, where they multiply. They infect red blood cells and multiply, and the rupture of RBCs releases merozoites and a toxin called haemozoin, which causes the chill and high fever. Some parasites develop into gametocytes.
keyPoints: Infect and burst RBCs, releasing merozoites
questions.explanation: Gametocytes are taken up by a mosquito, where sexual stages are completed.

questions.q: Butyric acid is produced by which bacterium?
questions.explanation: Clostridium butylicum gives butyric acid; Acetobacter aceti gives acetic acid.

questions.q: Which of the following drinks is produced by distillation of the fermented broth?
questions.explanation: Wine and beer are produced without distillation, while whisky, brandy and rum are obtained by distillation.

questions.q: The dough used for making idli and dosa gets puffed up because of:
options: Production of carbon dioxide by bacteria
questions.explanation: Bacteria in the fermented batter produce CO2, which causes it to puff.

questions.q: Which of the following fixes atmospheric nitrogen in paddy fields?
questions.explanation: Cyanobacteria such as Anabaena, Nostoc and Oscillatoria are autotrophic nitrogen fixers in paddy fields.

questions.q: Which result indicates that sewage treatment has been effective?
options: A marked decrease in the BOD of the effluent
questions.explanation: Microbes consume the organic matter, so BOD of the treated effluent falls.

questions.q: Lactic acid bacteria in the human gut are described as beneficial because they:
options: Check disease-causing microbes in the stomach
questions.explanation: LAB play a beneficial role in checking disease-causing microbes in the stomach.

questions.q: How does Rhizobium act as a biofertiliser for leguminous plants?
questions.answer: Rhizobium forms a symbiotic association with the roots of legumes and lives in root nodules. It fixes atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia and other organic forms that the plant can use, thus enriching the soil and reducing the need for chemical nitrogen fertilisers.
keyPoints: Symbiosis in root nodules of legumes
Reduces the need for chemical fertiliser
questions.explanation: Other examples of symbiotic nitrogen fixers include Frankia.

questions.q: Describe how a biogas plant works.
questions.answer: A biogas plant has a concrete tank (digester) into which slurry of cattle dung is fed. A floating cover collects the gas, and anaerobic methanogenic bacteria digest the slurry and produce methane-rich biogas. The gas is drawn through a pipe, and the spent slurry is removed and used as manure.
keyPoints: Gas collected in floating cover; spent slurry used as manure
questions.explanation: Biogas is a renewable fuel.

questions.q: In recombinant DNA technology, a vector is:
options: A DNA molecule used to carry a foreign gene into a host cell
questions.explanation: Plasmids and bacteriophages are examples of vectors used to carry foreign DNA.

questions.q: In the name EcoRI of a restriction enzyme, the first letter E stands for the genus:
questions.explanation: The first letter comes from the genus (Escherichia) and the next two from the species (coli).

questions.q: Restriction enzymes cut the two strands of DNA a little away from the centre of the palindrome. This generates:
questions.explanation: The staggered cut leaves short single-stranded sticky ends that can base-pair with complementary ends.

questions.q: A good cloning vector should have:
options: Many recognition sites for the same restriction enzyme
One or very few recognition sites for the restriction enzyme
questions.explanation: A single cloning site ensures that the vector is cut only once, so the foreign DNA can be inserted at a specific place.

questions.q: Primers are needed in PCR because:
options: They cut the DNA at specific sites
They provide energy for the reaction
DNA polymerase can only extend an existing primer and cannot start synthesis by itself
questions.explanation: Primers anneal to the template and give a 3'-OH end from which the polymerase adds nucleotides.

questions.q: A linear DNA molecule has two recognition sites for EcoRI. Complete digestion with EcoRI will produce how many fragments?
questions.explanation: Each cut in a linear molecule adds one fragment, so two cuts produce three fragments.

questions.q: State the three basic steps in genetically modifying an organism.
questions.answer: The steps are identification of the DNA with the desirable gene, introduction of the identified DNA into the host, and maintenance of the DNA in the host with its transfer to the progeny.
keyPoints: Identify DNA with the desired gene
Maintain it in the host and pass it on to progeny
questions.explanation: These steps form the basis of genetic engineering.

questions.q: Differentiate between upstream and downstream processing in biotechnology.
questions.answer: Upstream processing includes the preparation of the cell culture and the growth of cells in the bioreactor to produce the protein. Downstream processing is the separation and purification of the product after the biosynthetic stage, and includes formulation with preservatives and quality control testing before marketing.
keyPoints: Upstream: culture and expression in the bioreactor
questions.explanation: Downstream processing varies with each product.

questions.q: Insulin is used for the treatment of:
questions.explanation: Insulin regulates blood sugar and is given to patients with diabetes.

questions.q: The first clinical gene therapy, given in 1990, was for a four-year-old girl with:
questions.explanation: The girl had adenosine deaminase deficiency, which affects the immune system.

questions.q: A patent is:
options: A licence to use any resource freely
A right granted by a government to an inventor to prevent others from commercially using the invention
questions.explanation: Patents give inventors exclusive commercial rights for a period.

questions.q: Which of the following is a benefit of genetically modified crops?
options: Reduced efficiency of mineral use by plants
questions.explanation: GM crops can have improved nutrition, tolerance to stress, less need for pesticides and fewer post-harvest losses.

questions.q: Transgenic mice are being used to test the safety of the:
questions.explanation: Transgenic mice are used to test vaccine safety, and this reduces the need to use monkeys.

questions.q: Transgenic animals are used to test the toxicity of drugs because they:
options: Are made more sensitive to toxic substances, so results come in a shorter time
Do not need to be fed
questions.explanation: Such animals show toxic effects quickly, so the safety of the chemical can be tested faster.

questions.q: Mention two uses of transgenic animals.
questions.answer: They are used to study how genes regulate normal physiology and the development of diseases such as cancer. They are also used as models for human diseases, to produce biological products like human protein-enriched milk, to test vaccine safety and to test the toxicity of chemicals.
keyPoints: Study of gene function and disease models
questions.explanation: Any two valid uses are acceptable.

questions.q: State two ethical or safety concerns about the use of genetically modified organisms.
questions.answer: GM organisms may have unpredicted effects on the ecosystem, such as harming non-target organisms or affecting biodiversity. There are also concerns about the use of living organisms as patented products and the misuse of bio-resources, so bodies like GEAC examine the safety of GM research.
keyPoints: Patenting of living organisms and biopiracy
Need for regulation such as GEAC
questions.explanation: Biotechnology needs ethical evaluation.

questions.q: Which feature is seen in the desert plant Opuntia?
options: Stomata open during the day on the upper side
Leaves reduced to spines, with photosynthesis done by the flattened stem
questions.explanation: These are adaptations to reduce water loss in deserts.

questions.q: Cattle egrets foraging near grazing cattle, feeding on insects flushed out by the cattle, is an example of:
questions.explanation: The egrets benefit while the cattle are neither benefited nor harmed.

questions.q: The Mediterranean orchid Ophrys ensures its pollination by:
options: Resembling the female of a species of bee so that male bees attempt to mate with the flower
questions.explanation: The flower mimics a female bee, so the male bee is deceived and pollinates it.

questions.q: The three ecological age groups of a population are:
questions.explanation: Age structure is represented by pyramids showing these three groups.

questions.q: In a population of 500 individuals, 25 are born during one year. What is the per capita birth rate?
questions.explanation: Per capita birth rate = 25/500 = 0.05 offspring per individual per year.

questions.q: A population has a per capita birth rate of 0.04 and a per capita death rate of 0.01 per year, with no migration. What is the intrinsic rate of natural increase (r)?
Distinguish between habitat and niche.
questions.answer: A habitat is the physical place where an organism lives, with its particular set of environmental conditions. A niche is the functional role of the organism in the ecosystem, including the range of conditions it tolerates and the resources it uses. Many species can share a habitat but each has a different niche.
keyPoints: Niche: functional role and resources used
Many species share a habitat but not a niche
questions.explanation: Niche includes the way the organism interacts with biotic and abiotic factors.

questions.q: How do organisms cope with stressful external conditions when they can neither migrate nor regulate? Give examples.
questions.answer: Some organisms suspend their metabolic activity. Examples are hibernation of bears in winter, aestivation in snails and fishes in summer, diapause in zooplankton, and dormancy of seeds in plants. Spores of bacteria and fungi also help them survive harsh periods.
questions.explanation: Suspension lets organisms avoid stress in time.

questions.q: In the food chain grass -> deer -> tiger, the tiger is a:
questions.explanation: The deer is the primary consumer and the tiger, which eats it, is the secondary consumer.

questions.q: The network of interconnected food chains in an ecosystem is called a:
questions.explanation: Many food chains are linked together in nature to form a food web.

questions.q: The amount of nutrients such as carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus and calcium present in the soil at any given time is called the:
questions.explanation: The standing state is the amount of nutrients in the soil at a given time.

questions.q: Which one of the following nutrient cycles is a sedimentary cycle?
questions.explanation: Phosphorus and sulphur cycles are sedimentary, whereas carbon and nitrogen cycles are gaseous.

questions.q: In a forest ecosystem, the pyramid of biomass is generally:
questions.explanation: Large producer biomass supports smaller biomass at each higher trophic level, so the pyramid is upright.

questions.q: If 20 J of energy is available at the secondary consumer level, how much energy was fixed by the producers, using the ten percent law?
questions.explanation: Primary consumers had 20/0.1 = 200 J, and the producers had 200/0.1 = 2000 J.

questions.q: What are ecosystem services? Give three examples.
questions.answer: Ecosystem services are the products of ecosystem processes that benefit humans. Healthy ecosystems purify air and water, mitigate droughts and floods, cycle nutrients, generate fertile soil and provide wildlife habitat, and they also pollinate crops and regulate climate.
keyPoints: Benefits humans get from ecosystem processes
questions.explanation: Ecosystem services have a large economic value.

questions.q: Describe the stages of primary succession on a bare rock (xerarch succession).
questions.answer: Lichens are pioneers and secrete acids that weather the rock and form a little soil. Mosses then grow, followed by herbs, shrubs and finally trees. Each stage changes the environment for the next, and the process ends with a stable climax community.
keyPoints: Trees form a stable climax community
questions.explanation: Xerarch succession takes place in dry areas.

questions.q: Which group of animals has the largest number of described species?
questions.explanation: Insects make up more than 70 per cent of all the recorded animal species.

questions.q: The illegal introduction of the African catfish Clarias gariepinus for aquaculture is a threat to:
questions.explanation: This alien species is a threat to the indigenous catfishes of Indian rivers.

questions.q: Sacred groves are found in which of the following regions of India?
questions.explanation: Sacred groves exist in the Khasi and Jaintia hills of Meghalaya, the Aravalli hills of Rajasthan and the Western Ghats.

questions.q: The current 'sixth extinction' differs from the previous five mass extinctions in that it is:
options: Occurring at a much faster rate and mainly caused by human activities
questions.explanation: The present rate of extinction is 100 to 1000 times faster than in the pre-human period, and it is due to human activities.

questions.q: Species diversity within a particular community or habitat is called:
questions.explanation: Alpha diversity is within a community, beta is between communities and gamma is over the whole region.

questions.q: David Tilman's long-term experiments on plots showed that plots with more species:
options: Showed less year-to-year variation in total biomass
questions.explanation: More species gave greater stability, and the plots also showed higher productivity.

questions.q: What is meant by the 'evil quartet'? List its four components.
questions.answer: The 'evil quartet' is the name given to the four major causes of biodiversity loss. They are habitat loss and fragmentation, over-exploitation, alien species invasions and co-extinctions.
questions.explanation: The term was coined by Jared Diamond.

questions.q: Explain the species-area relationship and its importance.
questions.answer: Within a region, species richness increases with the area, but only up to a limit. On a log scale it is a straight line, log S = log C + Z log A. It shows that the destruction of habitats, which reduces area, will lead to loss of species.
keyPoints: Habitat area loss means species loss
questions.explanation: The relationship was described by Alexander von Humboldt.
